title: Endorsed by mom, last dance for West, a treasurer’s office loss, more in political notes
summary: The governor has not endorsed in the Anne Arundel County executive's race, but his mom has; Sen. Chris West gets a little misty-eyed while testifying for the last time; a stop-and-go debate on buses and voting; and more in political notes.
content:
by William J. Ford, Christine Condon and Bryan P. Sears, Maryland Matters March 5, 2026

by William J. Ford, Christine Condon and Bryan P. Sears, Maryland Matters March 5, 2026

The mom of Gov. Wes Moore (D) is backing a candidate for Anne Arundel County executive.

Joy Thomas Moore, a media and philanthropy professional, is throwing her support behind Anne Arundel County Council member Pete Smith in the Democratic primary.

“Over the past few years, I’ve spent more time than I’ve ever imagined in the worlds of politics and public service,” Moore said in the campaign video. “So I think I know the real deal — quality leadership and values — when I see it.”

Moore, who said she has been a resident of Anne Arundel County for three decades, goes on to praise Smith’s military and community service.

“He embodies the principles that I have always stood for, and that I always wanted to instill in my children and every child: Service before self. Courage in the face of risk. And humility in victory,” Moore said.

Smith, in a statement, welcomed the endorsement: “Joy Moore’s lived experience and knowledge is worthy of respect. I’m honored that she sees leadership qualities in me that can help our community, and I’m proud to have her support as we move forward.”

Smith is one of four Democrats vying to succeed Steuart Pittman, who can not seek a third term. Pittman endorsed his special assistant, James Kitchin, to succeed him. That endorsement came before the Maryland Democratic Party named Pittman its party leader.

Also running in the Democratic primary are Anne Arundel County Council member Allison Packard, who has the backing of retiring Sen. Pam Beidle (D-Anne Arundel), and Kyle Nembhard. Dave Crawford is the only Republican in the race.

Unlike his mom, Gov. Moore has not endorsed in the Democratic primary for county executive. A spokesperson for the Moore campaign declined comment.

Senate Bill 100 seems straightforward enough: Introduced at the request of the State Board of Elections, it would require public buses that travel within a half mile of early voting centers to drop off or pick up people from those places, allowing “passengers to embark and disembark at the entrance of the early voting center.”

But somehow, that sparked two days of debate in the Senate.

It began Wednesday, when Sen. Arthur Ellis (D-Charles) asked Sen. Cheryl Kagan (D-Montgomery), the bill’s floor manager,  what the bill does. After Kagan said it would help senior citizens or those with disabilities, Ellis read portions of letters from several nonprofit groups that said better access for residents with disabilities is still needed. He offered an amendment to ensure that an early voting center “provides an accessible path to the entrance doors” for those with physical disabilities.

A few minutes later, Sen. J.B. Jennings (R-Baltimore and Harford) rose to ask about buses that may have to turn corners on certain streets and have “to jump the curbs. I don’t actually find this feasible. I find it more dangerous…”

That didn’t sit well with Ellis, who told Jennings, “This is not silly season, OK? It’s not a joke.”

“Of course, if a bus can’t make into a location, the bus won’t go there, period. This is … insulting and I take that personally,” Ellis said. “Where the buses can go, make sure they go to location that’s accessible. Period. Full stop.”

Jennings said he wasn’t trying to be insulting or “make it a joke,” just that the amendment may have been “written erroneously” and he was willing to help rewrite it.

At that point, Sen. Brian Feldman (D-Montgomery), chair of the Education, Energy and the Environment Committee that presented the bill, asked for it to be held a day, and discussion ended.

It resumed Thursday when Ellis withdrew his amendment and presented a new one to ensure accessibility is “in accordance with the Americans with Disabilities Act.” Kagan said the bill already did that, and the majority of her colleagues appeared to agree, voting 34-9 to reject the amendment. The debate ended and bill received preliminary approval.

The Office of the Treasurer lost a member of staff over the weekend when Nakia R. Wright, executive assistant to Treasurer Dereck Davis, died unexpectedly Saturday morning. She was 51.

“That’s a tremendous loss for all of us,” Davis said during the Board of Public Works meeting Wednesday.

Davis first met Wright three years ago after being introduced by a departing member of the Prince George’s County Council. Wright was interested in filling the vacancy. Davis was already supporting a different candidate but agreed to meet with her.

“I talked to her and I saw why he was supporting her right away. She was very likable, smart, funny,” Davis said. “We had such great conversations about just a lot of things.”

Wright was also the first lady of The Gathering at Forestville Church. There was no information on the cause of death. Funeral arrangements were incomplete.

Sen. Chris West (R-Baltimore and Carroll) was nearly finished testifying for his bill on the state’s energy challenges when he realized something.

This would be his last bill hearing, well … ever.

“This is my final bill,” he said, pausing to hold back tears. “As I conclude my 12-year tenure. It’s also perhaps the most significant bill of my legislative career.”

West was testifying before the House Education, Energy and the Environment Committee on his bill, co-sponsored with Sen. Katie Fry Hester (D-Howard and Montgomery), to require the state to develop a list of five to 10 sites that would be suitable for the rapid development of energy generating facilities.  The Maryland Stadium Authority — which manages Camden Yards and M&T Bank stadiums, but has previously been asked to participate in other construction projects — would then conduct feasibility studies on each site.

During his presentation, West noted the massive power demand projections anticipated to hit PJM Interconnection, chiefly because of data centers. He fears that the grid could become overwhelmed, causing local blackouts.

“We can’t afford to start down the preferred path of an outspoken legislator, only to realize two or three years down the road that we’ve taken the wrong course,” West said. “The Stadium Authority has the credibility and the resources to draw on the wisdom of the smartest people in the energy sector.”

The Stadium Authority has tackled major projects from the renovation of the Hippodrome to school construction and local sports complexes.

Committee Chair Sen. Brian Feldman (D-Montgomery), noting that energy is among the most important subjects of the session, told West, “You picked the right topic, I would say, for a coup de grâce of your legislative career.”

Maryland first lady Dawn Moore made an unpublicized appearance in the Senate Finance Committee Thursday, joining a panel in support of Senate Bill 820. The bill, sponsored by Sen. Antonio Hayes (D-Baltimore City), bans the sale and marketing of kratom and related products and gives the Alcohol Tobacco and Cannabis Commission the authority to enforce the law and seize products.

Mrs. Moore’s appearance caught the attention of Sen. Ben Kramer (D-Montgomery), who said to Hayes that he “never had an interest in having the governor sit next to me at a bill hearing, but I will share with you that I am incredibly envious that you have the first lady sitting next to you at a bill hearing.”

Hayes is a friend of Gov. Wes Moore’s.

“I just want to know how I can make that happen because I am so jealous,” Kramer said.

The comment elicited laughter from the panel — including Dawn Moore — and others in the audience.

“And if I may, first lady, if you ever get bored with the governor … I’m just putting it out there,” Kramer said.

Again, more laughter.

The first lady later issued a press release about her testimony. There was no comment on Kramer’s, umm, offer.

— This story was updated on Friday, March 6, to correct Treasurer Dereck Davis’ title.
